title: Design Bounded Blocking Queue
description: Brute force to optimized: a naive busy-wait loop versus the classic mutex-plus-condition-variables producer-consumer synchronization pattern.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Implement a thread-safe BOUNDED BLOCKING QUEUE with a fixed capacity, supporting concurrent producer and consumer threads: enqueue(element) adds an element, BLOCKING (waiting, not failing) if the queue is currently full; dequeue() removes and returns the front element, BLOCKING if the queue is currently empty; size() returns the current number of elements. The queue must correctly coordinate MULTIPLE threads calling these methods concurrently, without corrupting its internal state or losing/duplicating elements.

blocks.caption: A capacity-limited queue where full/empty conditions cause a calling thread to WAIT (block) rather than fail, correctly resuming once the condition changes

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Block\" (wait), not fail, when a capacity condition is violated","Condition variables (or semaphores), which let a thread efficiently SLEEP until woken, rather than repeatedly checking in a busy-loop"],["Multiple threads accessing shared state concurrently","A mutex/lock protecting all access, ensuring no two threads corrupt the queue's internal state simultaneously"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

This is fundamentally a CONCURRENCY problem: multiple threads may call enqueue and dequeue simultaneously, and the queue must correctly coordinate them, making a thread WAIT (not error out) when the queue is momentarily full (for enqueue) or empty (for dequeue), efficiently waking it once the condition resolves.

blocks.title: A Note on This Judge's Simulation
blocks.text: Since this platform's judge executes solutions in a single, sequential process (reading operations from standard input one at a time), it cannot directly test TRUE multi-threaded blocking behavior. The version presented here for hands-on practice simulates the SEQUENCE of enqueue/dequeue/size calls in order, always guaranteed to be well-formed (no enqueue ever occurs while already at capacity, no dequeue ever occurs while empty), letting you focus on the underlying queue mechanics; the explanation below covers the FULL, real multi-threaded solution as it would be implemented in a genuine concurrent environment.

blocks.caption: A full queue makes an enqueuing thread wait; a dequeue frees a slot and wakes it; symmetrically, an empty queue makes a dequeuing thread wait until an enqueue wakes it

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: capacity = 2; enqueue(1), enqueue(2), dequeue(), dequeue()

blocks.title: In a truly concurrent scenario
blocks.text: If a THIRD enqueue(3) had been attempted while the queue was still at capacity [1,2], that calling thread would BLOCK (pause) until one of the dequeue() calls freed up space, then automatically proceed once woken.
5. How Should We Think?

Before using a naive "busy-wait" loop (repeatedly re-checking a condition in a tight loop, wasting CPU the entire time), notice that CONDITION VARIABLES let a thread efficiently sleep until a specific condition becomes true, waking up only when actually notified.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A shared mutable queue accessed by multiple threads needs a LOCK (mutex) to prevent simultaneous modifications from corrupting its internal state.

Observation 2: "Blocking" specifically means a thread should efficiently WAIT (not busy-loop, not error) when its desired operation cannot proceed yet; a condition variable is precisely the primitive designed for this: a thread can atomically release the lock and go to sleep, waking only when signaled.

Observation 3: Two DISTINCT waiting conditions exist here: "queue is full" (enqueue must wait) and "queue is empty" (dequeue must wait); using two separate condition variables (or one shared one, checked with different predicates) lets threads wait for exactly the right condition.

Observation 4: Whenever an operation CHANGES the condition that another thread might be waiting on (a dequeue frees a slot; an enqueue adds an item), that operation must NOTIFY the relevant waiting threads, so they can wake up and re-check their condition.

This is the classic producer-consumer synchronization pattern: a mutex protects shared state, and condition variables let threads efficiently wait for (and be notified of) specific state changes, rather than busy-waiting.
6. Brute Force Solution

Use a plain queue with a simple BUSY-WAIT loop for blocking: repeatedly check the condition in a tight loop until it becomes false, then proceed. (Shown here for a sequential simulation, since this platform cannot execute true concurrent threads; the loop illustrates the naive, inefficient concurrency approach conceptually.)
Step by step algorithm

items: enqueue: repeatedly check if the queue is full (in a tight loop, wasting CPU the whole time); once not full, add the element.
dequeue: repeatedly check if the queue is empty (same busy-wait pattern); once not empty, remove and return the front element.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The busy-wait loop directly (if inefficiently) implements "block until the condition changes," by simply re-checking repeatedly.

This approach is NOT thread-safe as written (no locking at all), and would waste enormous CPU resources if actually run concurrently, making it purely illustrative of the naive idea, not production-ready.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Conceptually blocks correctly (eventually proceeding once the condition changes), but is neither thread-safe (no locking around shared state) nor efficient (wastes CPU continuously while waiting).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per successful operation, but potentially UNBOUNDED wasted CPU cycles while busy-waiting.
Space: O(capacity), for the queue.
Limitation: lacks both thread-safety (a proper lock) and efficient waiting (condition variables instead of busy-waiting); a proper mutex-plus-condition-variable design solves both issues.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force busy-waits without any real locking. Instead, use a mutex to protect all access to the shared queue, plus condition variables for each waiting reason (not-full, for enqueue; not-empty, for dequeue). A thread that cannot proceed atomically releases the lock and sleeps efficiently via the condition variable's wait(), only re-checking once explicitly notified by the operation that changed the relevant condition.

Maintain a queue, a mutex, and (in languages without a single combined monitor) two condition variables. enqueue: acquire the lock; while full, wait on notFull; add the element; notify notEmpty. dequeue: acquire the lock; while empty, wait on notEmpty; remove the front element; notify notFull. size: acquire the lock; return the current count.
9. Optimized Solution
Use a mutex to protect shared state, and condition variables to let threads efficiently wait for (and be notified of) exactly the right condition change.
Conceptual trace for capacity = 2; threads calling enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), dequeue()

blocks.text: For the guaranteed-well-formed operation sequences this judge tests, size(), enqueue(), and dequeue() behave exactly like a standard capacity-bounded FIFO queue, since blocking never actually needs to occur.

codes.python:
import threading
from collections import deque

class BoundedBlockingQueue:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.queue = deque()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(self.lock)                     # signaled when a slot frees up (a dequeue happened)
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(self.lock)                    # signaled when an item arrives (an enqueue happened)

    def enqueue(self, element):
        with self.not_full:
            while len(self.queue) >= self.capacity:
                self.not_full.wait()                                       # sleeps efficiently, no CPU wasted, until notified
            self.queue.append(element)
            self.not_empty.notify()                                        # wake up one thread waiting to dequeue

    def dequeue(self):
        with self.not_empty:
            while len(self.queue) == 0:
                self.not_empty.wait()                                      # sleeps efficiently until notified
            val = self.queue.popleft()
            self.not_full.notify()                                         # wake up one thread waiting to enqueue
            return val

    def size(self):
        with self.lock:
            return len(self.queue)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bq = BoundedBlockingQueue(2)
    bq.enqueue(1)
    print(bq.size())
    bq.enqueue(2)
    print(bq.size())
    print(bq.dequeue())
    print(bq.dequeue())

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per operation once able to proceed (excluding legitimate wait time when actually blocked); no wasted CPU while waiting.
Space: O(capacity), for the queue.
Why This Works

The mutex ensures only ONE thread ever modifies the queue's internal state at a time, preventing corruption. Condition variables let a thread that cannot yet proceed release the lock and sleep EFFICIENTLY (using no CPU) until specifically notified, rather than repeatedly re-checking in a wasteful loop. Using the CORRECT condition variable (notFull vs. notEmpty) for each operation, and notifying the OPPOSITE one whenever an operation succeeds, correctly wakes exactly the threads that might now be able to proceed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["enqueue() when the queue is full","The calling thread waits on notFull, sleeping until a dequeue() frees a slot and notifies it"],["dequeue() when the queue is empty","The calling thread waits on notEmpty, sleeping until an enqueue() adds an item and notifies it"],["size()","Simply reads the current count under the lock, needing no waiting at all"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The wait() call on a condition variable is used in a WHILE loop (not a single if), since a woken thread must always RE-CHECK its condition (spurious wakeups, or another thread "stealing" the freed slot first, are both real possibilities in genuine concurrent systems).
Notifying the OPPOSITE condition variable after a successful operation (enqueue notifies notEmpty; dequeue notifies notFull) is what allows waiting threads on the OTHER operation to make progress.
The lock must be held for the ENTIRE check-wait-modify-notify sequence, ensuring no other thread can interleave and cause a race condition.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (busy-wait, no locking)","O(1) + wasted CPU while waiting","O(capacity)","Not thread-safe, and wastes CPU continuously while blocked"],["Optimized (mutex + condition variables)","O(1) + efficient (CPU-free) waiting","O(capacity)","Thread-safe and efficient: threads sleep rather than busy-loop"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Implementing a "blocking" concurrent data structure requires BOTH a lock (protecting shared state from simultaneous modification) AND condition variables (letting threads efficiently wait for, and be notified of, specific state changes), rather than a naive busy-wait loop.
Common mistakes

items: Using a single "if" check instead of a "while" loop around a condition-variable wait(), missing the need to RE-CHECK after waking (spurious wakeups or lost races are real possibilities).
Forgetting to notify the correct (opposite) condition variable after a successful operation, leaving waiting threads on the other side stuck forever.
Using a busy-wait loop for "blocking" instead of a genuine condition variable, wasting CPU resources continuously while a thread waits.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly naming this as "the producer-consumer pattern" and describing the mutex-plus-condition-variables design demonstrates recognizing this as a well-known, standard concurrency problem, not something to solve from first principles.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "A queue that BLOCKS (not fails) when full or empty, used by multiple threads" points directly to the mutex-plus-condition-variables producer-consumer pattern.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you implement this using SEMAPHORES instead of condition variables? Two counting semaphores (one tracking available slots, one tracking available items) directly model the same blocking behavior, often considered a cleaner fit for this specific bounded-buffer problem.

Why must the condition-variable wait be inside a WHILE loop, not an IF? Because a woken thread is not guaranteed the condition still holds by the time it actually resumes (another thread might have already consumed the available slot/item, or a spurious wakeup occurred), so it must re-verify before proceeding.

How would you extend this to support MULTIPLE producers and MULTIPLE consumers correctly? The same mutex-plus-condition-variables design already handles this correctly, since the lock serializes all access regardless of how many threads are involved, and notifying (rather than a single direct handoff) lets any waiting thread be the one to proceed.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The classic bounded-buffer producer-consumer synchronization pattern, a foundational concurrency problem distinct from the purely sequential queue-simulation problems elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) + wasted CPU while busy-waiting; O(capacity) space.
Optimized (mutex + condition variables): O(1) + efficient waiting; O(capacity) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Producer-consumer synchronization via a mutex and condition variables
Core Idea: A lock protects shared state; condition variables let a thread efficiently wait for a specific condition (not full / not empty), waking only when notified by the operation that changed it
Time: O(1) per operation (excluding legitimate wait time)
Space: O(capacity)
Most Important Observation: A woken thread must RE-CHECK its condition in a while loop, never assuming it can immediately proceed just because it was notified
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Lock + while(condition) wait(); modify; notify(the opposite condition)
